headline: HSC pass rate hits 20-year low at 52.12%, exposing major learning gaps
summary: Bangladesh's Higher Secondary Certificate (HSC) and equivalent examinations recorded their lowest pass rate since 2004, prompting education officials to acknowledge significant shortcomings in teaching and learning methods.
details: Bangladesh's Higher Secondary Certificate (HSC) and equivalent examinations have revealed their worst results in over two decades, exposing deep-seated weaknesses in the education system that officials say can no longer be overlooked. This year's outcome has left authorities both disappointed and surprised.

Only 52.12 percent of candidates successfully passed the examinations, marking the lowest pass rate recorded since 2004. Out of the successful candidates, 40,084 students achieved a GPA-5, which accounts for 6.2 percent of those who passed.

Compared to last year, the pass rate has dropped by 6.71 percentage points, and the number of GPA-5 achievers has fallen significantly by 29,013. Officials attribute this decline to identified learning gaps, inconsistent teaching standards, and a stricter assessment process.

Education Advisor Mahdi Amin stated that the government ensured impartial marking in these examinations, the first under the newly elected administration. He also announced that a full re-evaluation process would be implemented for the first time, aiming for the highest recognition based on student performance.

The education ministry is exploring the possibility of holding fresh examinations within a month for students who failed in one or two subjects. Education Minister ANM Ehsanul Hoque Milon acknowledged deficiencies in learning methods, parental involvement, and the overall educational environment, urging reassessment and active participation from parents and teachers.

The examinations, which began on July 2 and concluded on August 8, faced disruptions including postponements in five Chattogram board districts due to natural disasters. Student protests in Dhaka demanded deferment of exams, leading to road blockades and clashes with police.

Subject-wise analysis across the nine general education boards showed particularly poor performances in English and Accounting, with pass rates often ranging between 52 and 59 percent. Information and Communication Technology (ICT) results were comparatively better, with most boards reporting pass rates above 60 percent.

The Barishal Board recorded the lowest overall pass rate at 44.84 percent, largely due to low scores in English (54.08%) and Accounting (52.20%). Rajshahi board also saw a low pass rate of 45.06 percent. Officials like Prof Sharif Morshed Reza expressed disappointment, citing potential shortcomings among teachers and commercial interests in certain subjects.

topic: father cries over deceased son hsc result
headline_marked: [[Father breaks down seeing deceased son's HSC results]] for exam he couldn't complete
headline: Father breaks down seeing deceased son's HSC results for exam he couldn't complete
summary: Minhajul Islam Rozan passed away before completing his HSC practical exams, making his father's grief even more profound upon seeing the published results.
details: Minhajul Islam Rozan, a student of Bangladesh International School and College (BISC) in Dhaka Cantonment, passed away before he could see his HSC exam results. His father, Sajjadul Miraj, broke down in tears on Saturday after seeing the published results. Rozan had passed all subjects except biology practicals, which he couldn't attend due to illness.

Rozan achieved a GPA of 4.33 in all subjects except Biology. Had he been able to take the practical exam and scored an A+ in Biology, his final GPA would have been 4.83, according to his father. The results were sent to his father by a school teacher.

Rozan fell ill on August 12 during his HSC practical exams and was on life support for ten days before succumbing to his illness. His parents expressed regret over the circumstances surrounding his illness and death.

His parents, Sajjadul Miraj and Fahmida Akter, revealed they were unaware their son had diabetes, attributing his initial symptoms to exam stress or panic attacks. They allege that necessary tests, including for diabetes, were not conducted initially.

On August 13, while on life support at Shahid Suhrawardy Medical College Hospital in Dhaka, Rozan's blood sugar level dangerously spiked to 38 mmol/L. This was the first time his parents learned about his diabetes.

The family shared that Rozan was an exemplary student, serving as class captain for five consecutive years from eighth to twelfth grade. He was also actively involved with the Bangladesh National Cadet Corps (BNCC), earning the trust of teachers and love of classmates.
